1:
Why cattle stand for theft in general they answer alike. Gill says the substance of men lay in oxen and sheep, named perhaps because they served for sacrifice as well as labour; Ellicott makes flocks and herds their principal property and reads the killing or selling as proof of a settled purpose. The unequal penalty is the puzzle. Henry and Wesley both say five is required for an ox because the owner lost its daily labour, and Henry draws the moral that fraud never enriches, since what is unjustly got will waste itself and consume what was our own with it. Ellicott confesses the principle is not clear and guesses that stealing an ox took more audacity and so more guilt. Calvin canvasses all three and settles on none: he doubts the argument from the ox's labour, thinks those nearer the truth who punish the boldness of taking the larger animal under witnesses' eyes, but judges it likelier that the difference followed the value of the beast, since he who does most harm should bear most punishment. Clarke cuts under the question by attacking the version, which renders two different Hebrew words by ox and two more by sheep; on his reading a man who steals a bull restores five oxen, hardly more than the animal's worth in a country without horses.

Calvin opens the civil laws with a comparison. Their principle, he says, is not so exact as what went before, God having relaxed his severity for the people's hardness; yet the heathen borrowed from them, and wherever Solon or the Decemvirs varied they changed for the worse. He instances the Roman rule, which fined the thief caught with the goods on him at fourfold and the other at double, on the reasoning that a man who does not fear disgrace is the bolder; God reverses it, taking double where the goods are found and fourfold where they have been killed or sold.

The burglar killed in the dark they justify on the ground of what cannot be known. Keil quotes the reason: the power and intention of a night thief are uncertain, and whether he came to murder; thieves resisted in the dark often turn to it, and can be neither recognised nor safely taken. Ellicott says most codes allow the inmates to resist and shed his blood, such a man having dissolved the social compact and made himself a public enemy; by day there is nothing to fear. Calvin argues the same from necessity, since no one can enter a house by night without digging through a wall or forcing a door, so that he can hardly be told from a robber; and where the Twelve Tables allowed the killing by day if the thief drew a weapon, God condemns to death the man who avenges a daylight theft with murder. Gill reports the rabbinic rule that a man entering with a digging tool is judged by his intent. Clarke and Ellicott both note that English law draws the same line, Clarke adding that the malignity lies less in the darkness than in the hour when sleep has disarmed the owner. Henry states the principle: a man's house is his castle, and God's law as well as man's sets a guard on it, so that he who assaults it does so at his peril — yet we ought to be tender even of bad men's lives. On the insolvent thief Ellicott has him become the six years' slave of the man he robbed, and Calvin notes that Rome did the same, quoting Cato on private thieves living in irons and public ones in gold and purple. Henry compares the sale to the transporting of felons, where alone Englishmen know what slavery is; Wesley repeats him and then corrects him, that the sentence is banishment and not slavery, no Englishman being sold unless he first indents himself.
5:
Trespass follows theft, and Ellicott gives the principle behind both. Only two kinds are given, but the rule appears: accidental injury, such as a fire running into another man's ground, was made good to the amount of the damage, while voluntary injury, such as turning beasts into a neighbour's field, was more than made good out of the offender's best. Calvin ranks the offence with theft — a man who sets his servant to steal is guilty though he touched nothing, and no less he who lets a brute do it — but restricts the penalty to twofold. On the phrase about the best of his field he takes his own line, and admits no commentator goes with him: he would have the ground surveyed and an award made by the utmost it would have yielded, where the others read restitution in kind out of the offender's best. Gill reads the first clause by the second, the field being eaten by cattle put in to feed; and on the fire he cites Jarchi for its breaking out even of itself. Wesley reports the rabbinic rule that restitution must always be of the best.

The fire they treat as a case of carelessness rather than malice. Clarke cites Harmer for the eastern custom of firing the dry herbage before the autumn rains, which for want of care often does great damage; Ellicott makes it the seasonal burning of weeds and farm refuse, done in Italy and England too, and notes how easily it spreads into a neighbour's crops. Keil identifies the thorns as the hedge round a cornfield and takes the case as unintentional injury. Calvin marks the difference from what precedes: the man who maliciously fired a cornfield was punished far more severely, and what is dealt with here is heedlessness. He raises the obvious defence, that a man could not foresee the thorns catching, and answers that God imposes the penalty of negligence precisely so that every man may take as much care of his neighbour's property as of his own. Wesley puts it as a maxim: he who meant only to burn thorns may become accessory to the burning of corn, men suffering for carelessness as well as malice, and answering not only for the hurt they do but for the hurt they occasion.

On goods left in trust they gather parallels from every side. Ellicott says the practice was widespread where there were no bankers, and Gill that the Targum takes it of a deposit kept freely, without reward. Clarke calls it pledging in the law of bailments, and notes that Rome made the depositary pay full value, double where the goods had been lodged under necessity. Keil describes the procedure when no thief is found: the householder goes before the court to clear himself of having laid hands on his neighbour's goods, which could only be done by an oath — and the Septuagint and Vulgate make that explicit by inserting the swearing, as Ellicott reports from Kalisch too. Calvin explains why so much rests on that oath. Depositaries cannot be required to do more than keep the thing as a prudent man keeps his own; to make one good the loss of a garment would be to put him in the thief's place. But an animal is not easily taken from the stall or the shepherd's hands, so its loss betrays the keeper's negligence unless violence can be shown. To the objection that the oath is too indulgent he answers that nobody entrusts property except to a man he thinks honest, and so has already testified against himself. Henry adds the morals — that we should keep another's goods as our own, that an oath ends strife because it appeals to God as avenger and not only as witness, and that no one should suffer for what he could not help.
9:
The action itself is what Calvin fastens on. Theft may be prosecuted, he says, but with a fine attached to a rash accusation; a man who suspects his neighbour may summon him and, proving his case, recover double, but if the judges find the charge groundless he pays the penalty himself, the suit carrying infamy as well as loss. Ellicott calls it a challenge at the challenger's risk, forfeiting double what he claimed if he fails. He renders the opening not as trespass generally but as every case of fraud, and remarks that the depositing of animals is unknown in classical antiquity though natural among a people whose wealth was in flocks; the case supposed is a trustee calling a thing lost which the depositor says he can identify. Clarke gives the practical reason for going to law: the man found with the goods may have bought them honestly. Calvin adds a note on the word for judges, properly a plural for gods, applied to dignify an office in which they stand in God's room — the reason, he says, that Christ calls them gods.

Gill gives the rabbinic scheme of four keepers: he who keeps for nothing, the borrower, the hirer and the man who takes hire. The first clears himself by oath; the borrower pays for everything; the two who deal for money swear as to what is torn or driven off or dies, but pay for what is lost or stolen. Ellicott distinguishes the three misfortunes — a natural death, a hurt from a wild beast or a fall, a driving off by the desert tribes — and observes that both might agree the animal had disappeared and dispute only how, so that the trustee brought proof if he could and swore if he could not. Keil and Ellicott explain the line: theft was reckoned preventable, a wild beast or an accident not. Clarke reflects on the oath. So solemn were appeals to God then that a man was taken for innocent who could swear he had not laid a hand on his neighbour's goods; oaths have since been so multiplied on trifles that their solemnity is gone, and will only return when they are used as sparingly as in Moses' day. Calvin values the phrase as showing the lawful use of an oath, men in hidden matters calling God to witness and by his name ending strife; the owner accepting it means he must acquiesce, and the oath being between them both, that God presides as judge and avenger.

The torn beast is proved by remains. Clarke would render the verse not as bringing the carcase but as bringing evidence of it, and reports the same rule among graziers, who must produce the horns and hoofs of a beast the dogs are said to have eaten, the owner's mark being there. Ellicott adds that such proof was not always possible, and that where it failed the trustee still had the oath. On the borrowed animal Calvin marks a wide distinction from a thing deposited, since he who lends confers a favour, so that a borrower binds himself to restore it safe as far as in him lies; but where the owner witnessed the death or injury he bears the loss, his presence answering that no fault of the borrower's caused it. Keil states it more shortly: the owner present either sees the thing could not have been prevented, or did not prevent it himself. Wesley turns it into a rule of conscience: we should not abuse what is lent us, since to do so is base as well as unjust, and should far rather lose ourselves than let anyone suffer for a kindness to us. Ellicott closes with the hired beast, akin to lending and yet another thing, the hirer not making good the damage, the risk being reckoned into the price.
16:
The case is carefully bounded. Gill points out that a girl might be betrothed without the marriage being consummated, and such a one counted as a wife, so the law supposes her neither betrothed nor forced but won by entreaty and promise. Clarke calls the provision wise and humane, and a check on seduction, since a man who thought of taking advantage knew he must marry the girl and endow her if her parents agreed, and pay a virgin's full dowry if they refused; the Targum fixes it at fifty shekels, and he could never divorce her after. Ellicott gives the reasoning from the father's side: he looked for a handsome sum from any man he betrothed his daughter to, so that if the seducer was beneath him he might exact enough to induce another to wed her, and if not, compel the marriage. Calvin notes that though the judicial penalty is remitted, fornication still displeases God, and finds the law's point in protecting young women, lest having been deceived they turn prostitutes and defile the land; the dowry is required so that if cast off she may not go penniless. Henry and Wesley draw the same moral, that even where the divine law appoints the marriage, both as punishment and recompense, the father's power is reserved: if he withholds consent there is no marriage, which shows how ill a thing it is for children to marry without it.

On the witch they divide. Gill supposes that such women conversed with familiar spirits and appeared to raise the dead, though in reality they could not — the witch of Endor's astonishment at Samuel proving the thing outside her practice — so that they are condemned as deceivers who drew the people from depending on God. Clarke argues the other way and thinks the law itself proof of the reality, since it would never have been made had there been no witches; scripture, he holds, represents such persons as really evoking the dead, and he derives the Hebrew word from a root meaning to uncover. Ellicott declines the question: whether they had help from evil spirits or only professed it, the sin was the same, Jehovah being renounced and another power invoked. The word, he notes, is a feminine of the term used for the sorcerers of Egypt and means a mutterer of charms. Calvin answers the same point: the crime is no more tolerable in a man, and the law is directed at women because their sex is the more disposed to superstition. Wesley closes with the sharpest word in the chapter: our law once made such dealings felony without benefit of clergy, but we are wiser than our forefathers, and believe no witch ever lived at all.

The two remaining crimes are dispatched with distaste. Of the beast Gill says the thing is so dishonourable to human nature that one would think no law against it could be needed, and only the depravity of mankind made divine wisdom see otherwise. Clarke and Ellicott both take its mention as evidence that it was practised, Clarke suspecting an Egyptian custom and citing a traveller for its continuance there, Ellicott finding it common among the Canaanites, so that God's abhorrence had to be declared. On the sacrificer Gill takes the word for gods to cover every object of idolatrous worship, and especially the sun, moon and stars; Ellicott says sacrifice here stands for worship generally, being its chief act. Clarke, Ellicott and Keil agree on the force of the word rendered utterly destroyed: it is the ban, a thing finally separated from God and devoted to destruction beyond redemption — the man being by that death devoted to the Lord he would not devote himself to in life. Henry thinks the law might have prevented the later apostasies of the nation, had those who should have executed it not led the breach.
21:
Who the stranger is they define. Gill offers two senses — a man not born in the country, come in for trade or driven by some providence, or else a proselyte, and not the proselyte of righteousness but the proselyte of the gate, who has taken on himself the commandments of the sons of Noah. Such men were suffered to dwell among Israel, and the vexing forbidden is chiefly with words: calling them Gentiles or uncircumcised, upbraiding them with their country or their former life, or telling a proselyte to remember his old works and a proselyte's son his father's. Keil sets the command against what precedes — they were not to sacrifice to foreign gods, but the foreigner himself they were not merely to tolerate but not to vex — and observes that as a man without rights he is commended to their kindness by their own memory of Egypt. Clarke calls the law humane and the fruit of sound policy: treat strangers well and many will take refuge with you, so the strength of the country is increased, and being well used they may become proselytes; justice, humanity, policy and religion all say the same. Ellicott turns the reason into a duty, that they should not merely refrain from vexing but love the stranger as themselves, and points to evidence that foreigners fared more than tolerably in Israel — the Kenites, Araunah the Jebusite, Uriah the Hittite.

Wesley enumerates what vexing includes: wronging a stranger in judgment, imposing on him in contracts, taking advantage of his necessity, or merely upbraiding him with it. He then draws out the reason given, that they had been strangers in Egypt and knew what it was to be oppressed, and makes it a rule — men who have been in distress, if providence enriches them, owe a tenderness to those now in the case they were in once, doing by them as they then wished to be done by. On the widow and the fatherless Gill explains why these two are named when the law binds all alike: they have no husband or father to take their side, being unable to defend themselves, so that cruel men take advantage of it. Keil takes the verb for afflicting to cover not merely oppression but every kind of cold and contemptuous treatment. Wesley reads the prohibition as a command in disguise: not to afflict them means to comfort and assist them, and in making just demands their condition must be weighed — people unversed in business, destitute of advice, timorous and tender-spirited, needing the compassion a father would have sheltered them with.

The sanction is what strikes them most. Clarke remarks that offences against this law are not left to the judges' discretion: God reserves the punishment to himself, and by that shows how he abhors the crime, which is no common one and shall not be punished in a common way; the man who helps a widow or an orphan does a service highly acceptable to him. Gill spells out the affliction — reproaches to the mind, stripes or false imprisonment to the body, and to the substance the withholding of what belongs to them — and notes that the Hebrew doubles the verb, so the sense is to afflict them much and keep on. Ellicott renders both clauses so: if thou afflict them sore, and they cry earnestly unto me. He then reads the threat forward, listing the prophets who charge the later Israelites with breaking these very laws, and concludes that the sword of the Babylonians and afterwards of the Romans avenged the sufferers, as this verse had said. Keil states the mechanism: such forsaken ones stand under Jehovah's special watchfulness, and he takes their troubles on himself and repays their oppressors. Gill closes on the aggravation, that the circumstances of the persons ill treated make the injustice the more provoking.
25:
What the word means is disputed first. Clarke derives it from a root meaning to bite, so that the Latins rightly called such gain devouring usury: the increase resembles a serpent's bite, scarcely felt at first, but the venom spreads until it reaches the vitals. He takes the verse of compound interest, and defines usury as more than the law allows. Ellicott flatly denies the distinction: the two Hebrew words carry no sense of excess, but mean simply interest and the man who lends on it. Gill notes the rabbinic limitation, that the law respects Israelites only, the poor man meant being the poor man who is with thee. Calvin heads off another misreading: the question is not usury as some have supposed, as if lending were commanded to be gratuitous, but that men lend only to the rich from whom they expect a return, whereas charity is proved by lending where no return can be looked for. Before he comes to loans, he observes, God speaks of poverty to dispose men's minds to pity, using the figure of a man tottering who is to be held up by the hand; and what follows about the stranger extends the rule, since if humanity is not denied to foreigners, much more is help owing to a brother.

How far the law still binds is the next question. Henry and Wesley answer it in the same words. They may not take interest from a man borrowing for necessity, and since a people with little concern in trade could hardly borrow for anything else, the thing is forbidden among themselves, though lending to a stranger was allowed; so that in strictness the law seems peculiar to the Jewish state. In the equity of it it still binds us to show mercy where we have the advantage, and to share loss as well as profit with those we lend to — and on that condition, they argue, it seems as lawful to take interest for money another works with and risks in trade as to take rent for land another works in husbandry. Calvin reaches a partly opposite conclusion. He grants the precept is political, its Jewish form proved by the liberty to take interest of Gentiles; the judicial law is abrogated only so far that charity's dictate remains, that brethren in need are not to be treated harshly. But because the wall between Jew and Gentile is now broken down, our case is altered, and we must spare all without exception — the household of faith holding the first place, but the common society of mankind forbidding us to grow rich by another's loss. Clarke praises the English law that voids the bond and forfeits treble the sum where usury is proved, and remarks tartly that the people for whom this law was made practise it still.

The pledge and its return they treat concretely. Gill observes that the lender might not impose interest and yet might take the borrower's clothes or tools as security. Clarke finds it strange that a pledge should be taken which must so quickly be given back, and supposes it was returned only for the night; the rabbins hold that a man had the use of whatever was needful even while pawned, working with his tools by day and carrying them back at evening. He identifies the garment with the hyke, a coarse blanket an Arab still sleeps on. He adds a second use for the daily return: it acknowledged the debt afresh, standing in place of a written bond. Keil quotes the reason the text gives, that the garment is his covering for his skin, and asks what else he is to wrap himself in. Gill puts it plainest — it is all he has to cover him — and fixes the hour by the labourer's day, who comes home at sunset and lies down.
28:
What the word for gods means is the chapter's sharpest dispute. Gill reports the reading of Philo and Josephus, that the heathen deities are meant, but rejects it as contrary to scripture. He takes it of the civil magistrates, powers ordained of God, and cites the Targum and Aben Ezra for judges. Wesley says the same, adding that magistrates are our fathers, whom the fifth commandment obliges us to honour, and that Paul owned he ought not to speak evil of the ruler of his people, though that ruler persecuted him. Clarke reports the common view and refuses it: the original should be understood of the true God only, so that the verse forbids making light of God and cursing the ruler who derives his authority from him. Ellicott sets out both sides. The Greek and Latin versions gave the first sense and Philo and Josephus expounded it so, the latter boasting that Jews abstained from reviling the gods of the nations; but the practice of the most pious Israelites was otherwise, and the heathen gods are reviled everywhere with scorn. Against the second sense he raises a point of grammar, that the word would need the article to mean judges, and renders it God, taking the passage to join the sin of cursing a ruler to that of reviling God, the ruler being his representative. Calvin gets the same result another way, that the two clauses say one thing twice in the Hebrew manner, so that the gods and the rulers are the same persons.

Calvin then presses the title. These passages, he says, confirm that all superiors are comprised in the fifth commandment; the name of God is applied to magistrates figuratively but reasonably, since he has stamped a mark of his glory on his ministers, so that they are to be obeyed not from fear of punishment but for conscience' sake. To the objection that this praises men who abuse their power, he answers that their honour is no cover for their faults, and that the people should deplore what is wrong in silence rather than overturn government.

On the first-fruits Gill reports the rabbinic limits — seven kinds only, wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives and dates — the quantity left to the giver, the bountiful bringing a fortieth, the covetous a sixtieth. Keil renders the two words as the produce of the corn and of the press, the second being literally a flowing or a tear; Calvin argues the same against those who assign one word to wine and the other to oil, so that not only the fruit but the drops pressed from it were to be offered. Ellicott calls first-fruits the spontaneous tribute of natural piety among almost all nations, and observes that here they are assumed due, the stress falling on offering them promptly. Clarke gathers the pagan parallels: Censorinus on the ancients consecrating part of everything to the gods, to prove themselves grateful rather than because the gods needed it, and Pliny on the Romans tasting no new corn before the priests had offered. Wesley draws the application, that we have much more reason to give ourselves and all we have to God, who spared not his own Son, and warns that delaying a duty risks omitting it. Clarke and Ellicott both explain the seven days by the mother's health, Clarke adding that the Romans reckoned lambs impure before the eighth day. Of the torn flesh Clarke gives the reason as the blood, coagulated in the meat and held sacred from Noah's day; Wesley adds the defilement by the touch of the unclean beast, and Ellicott both, remarking that it might be sold to an alien. Keil takes the whole as the nation showing itself holy, and Clarke closes on that word: no command was issued from mere sovereignty, but all as restraints on disorderly passions and incentives to holiness.
